clue.text: Aden with red wallpaper for Conan Doyle?

parts.note: taken as written
a den is a private room for reading and work, a study
a room papered in red is dressed in scarlet

explanation.surface: A question about the decor of a novelist's private room, papered in red.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'Aden' is the words 'A den' run together. The definition with its question mark points to a Conan Doyle title, the first Sherlock Holmes novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The first Sherlock Holmes novel was written by Arthur Conan Doyle, so the clue's question names one of his books.

parts.words: The — temperament is a disease that affects amateurs.. chesterton "
parts.note: a quotation from G. K. Chesterton with one word missing: the adjective for a creative temperament

explanation.surface: A quip by G. K. Chesterton about dabblers who fancy themselves creative.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Chesterton wrote that this temperament is a disease that afflicts amateurs.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word describes the creative, painterly temperament, the one Chesterton mocked in amateurs.

clue.text: Webster's shall go crazy defining du Maurier book

indicators.note: going crazy means the letters of these words are thrown into disorder and rearranged

parts.note: the S of the possessive is used as a letter here
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dictionary maker gets carried away while defining a novel by Daphne du Maurier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crazy' rearranges all fifteen letters of WEBSTERS SHALL GO, the possessive S included.
explanation.definitionFit: Daphne du Maurier wrote a 1963 novel about a family of French glassmakers under that title.

clue.text: "Marry, he must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil", he said

definitions.text: "Marry, he must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil", he said

parts.words: "Marry, he must have a long spoon that must eat with the devil", he said
parts.note: asks who speaks this line in Shakespeare's The Comedy of Errors

explanation.surface: A proverb about supping with the devil, attributed to an unnamed speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is spoken in The Comedy of Errors by the servant of Antipholus of Syracuse.
explanation.definitionFit: The speaker of the proverb is a Shakespearean servant, one of a pair of identical twins in The Comedy of Errors.

clue.text: Strangely cool antics of heretic

indicators.note: strangely says the letters of the following words are arranged in an odd new order

explanation.surface: A heretic behaving with oddly calm antics.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions is a heretic in a broad sense.

clue.text: Like a Burroughs machine

parts.note: points to the adjective in the title of William S. Burroughs's 1961 novel about a machine

explanation.surface: Describing a device made by the Burroughs adding-machine company.
explanation.walkthrough: Burroughs was also a maker of office calculating machines, but the clue means William S. Burroughs's novel The ___ Machine.
explanation.definitionFit: William S. Burroughs titled his 1961 cut-up novel after a pliant, yielding machine.

clue.text: Few, perhaps, providing wind power required by 2?

explanation.surface: Asking whether a little breath would be enough for the craftsmen of the earlier clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Few' were the RAF pilots of the Battle of Britain, after Churchill's speech. Read literally, the answer is the force of air that glassblowers need.
explanation.definitionFit: Churchill's 'Few' were fighter pilots of the military flying service, and glassblowers need a stream of breath with real strength behind it.

clue.text: No score in Ian McEwan novel by Nicholas reeling 7

parts.note: in tennis a score of nil is called love
taken as written
Ian McEwan won the 1998 Booker Prize for his novel Amsterdam

explanation.surface: Nil points for a McEwan novel, set against a detective writer.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'Nicholas reeling 7' is a misreading of 'Nicolas Freeling?', the Dutch-detective author.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicolas Freeling's first Van der Valk detective story, published in 1962, carries this title.

clue.text: Oppressor associated with a lady by Gilbert Parker

definitions.text: associated with a lady by Gilbert Parker

explanation.surface: A cruel ruler linked with a heroine in a romantic novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert Parker, the Canadian novelist, wrote The Lady and the ___.
explanation.definitionFit: A despot is a cruel oppressor, and Gilbert Parker paired one with a lady in a novel's title.

clue.text: Venetian artist shows attachment to Venetian traveller

parts.note: a tie is a bond or attachment
Marco Polo was the Venetian who travelled to China

explanation.surface: A Venetian painter shows fondness for a fellow citizen who journeyed far.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was the great eighteenth-century painter of Venice.

clue.text: Always like Miss Winsor's signal to wait

definitions.text: like Miss Winsor's signal to wait

explanation.surface: A traffic light that, like Kathleen Winsor's heroine, stays at amber.
explanation.walkthrough: Kathleen Winsor wrote the bestseller Forever Amber; amber is the traffic light signal to wait.
explanation.definitionFit: Eternally means at all times, and Winsor's heroine is called '___ Amber', amber also being the traffic light colour.

clue.text: His best work was over the weekend

definitions.text: His best work was over the weekend

parts.words: His best work was over the weekend
parts.note: suggests a lazy worker but points to the author of Saturday Night and Sunday Morning

explanation.surface: A dig at someone who only produces anything good on Saturday and Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: Alan Sillitoe's best-known novel is Saturday Night and Sunday Morning, set across a weekend.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nottingham novelist is best remembered for a book whose title spans Saturday and Sunday.

clue.text: Gray, he was, and even older than he looked

definitions.text: Gray, he was, and even older than he looked

parts.words: Gray, he was, and even older than he looked
parts.note: refers to Oscar Wilde's ageless hero whose portrait aged instead of him

explanation.surface: A grey-haired man who was even older than he appeared.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gray' seems to mean grey-haired, but it is the surname of Wilde's hero, who stays young while his portrait ages.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's Dorian Gray kept his youthful looks while his hidden portrait recorded his true age and sins.

clue.text: "— — belongeth to them that are of full age" (Hebrews)

definitions.text: "— — belongeth to them that are of full age" (Hebrews)

parts.words: "— — belongeth to them that are of full age" (Hebrews)
parts.note: a quotation from Hebrews 5:14 in the King James Bible with two words missing

explanation.surface: A Bible verse on what is fit for grown-ups.
explanation.walkthrough: The King James Bible contrasts milk for babes with this solid food for adults.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means solid food, and figuratively hard doctrine fit only for the mature.

clue.text: Sister of Shaun the Post and Shem the Penman recalling Paris suburb

definitions.text: Sister of Shaun the Post and Shem the Penman

explanation.surface: Recalling the sister of two brothers, a postman and a writer.
explanation.walkthrough: In Joyce's Finnegans Wake, Shaun and Shem have a sister; Issy-les-Moulineaux is a suburb of Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce named the daughter of Finnegans Wake after a diminutive of Isabel, which is also the short name of a Paris suburb.

clue.text: A Tarkington riche, not quite as nouveau as an Amberson

definitions.text: A Tarkington riche, not quite as nouveau as an Amberson

parts.note: points to a Booth Tarkington novel about a wealthy man, the author also of The Magnificent Ambersons

explanation.surface: Comparing two of Booth Tarkington's wealthy characters by how new their money is.
explanation.walkthrough: Booth Tarkington wrote The Plutocrat (1927) as well as The Magnificent Ambersons.
explanation.definitionFit: A person whose power comes from great wealth, the title figure of a Tarkington novel.

clue.text: Tenor magus

explanation.surface: A singer who is also a wise man.
explanation.walkthrough: Lauritz Melchior was a famous Danish tenor; by tradition one of the three Magi bore the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Danish Wagnerian singer and one of the three wise men of the Nativity share this name.

clue.text: A nemesis reorchestrated by French composer

explanation.surface: A French composer rescores a piece about vengeance.
explanation.definitionFit: Olivier Messiaen was a twentieth-century French composer and organist.

clue.text: Splendid preoccupation of Douglas

explanation.surface: A man called Douglas with a marvellous fixation.
explanation.walkthrough: Lloyd C. Douglas wrote the novel Magnificent Obsession (1929); 'Splendid' replaces 'Magnificent'.
explanation.definitionFit: A preoccupation is a fixation, and Douglas's novel calls it magnificent.

clue.text: Venus chose the fairest one, Dryden wrote

definitions.text: Venus chose the fairest one, Dryden wrote

parts.words: Venus chose the fairest one, Dryden wrote
parts.note: recalls the song in Dryden and Purcell's King Arthur in which Venus praises Britain

explanation.surface: Dryden recording the goddess of love picking the most beautiful one.
explanation.walkthrough: In King Arthur Venus sings 'Fairest Isle, all isles excelling', choosing Britain as her seat; it looks like the judgment of Paris.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryden's Venus praises Britain as the fairest of all islands.

clue.text: Lorenzo's father-in-law's profession

explanation.surface: Asking what trade a man's wife's father followed.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merchant of Venice Lorenzo elopes with Jessica, daughter of the moneylender Shylock.
explanation.definitionFit: Shylock lends money at interest, which is the trade of a moneylender.

clue.text: Endless row with two companies results in 9's style

parts.note: a line of things is a row

indicators.note: two asks for the following abbreviation to be written twice

explanation.surface: A never-ending quarrel involving two firms produces a particular artistic manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' cuts ROW to RO; '9' is the answer at 9-across, the Venetian painter Tiepolo.

clue.text: Impassive chaps like Zeno and Cleanthes

clue.text: Last product of Dekker's Eyre

clue.text: Once poured on a clown's head by Yorick

explanation.walkthrough: In Hamlet the gravedigger recalls that Yorick 'poured a flagon of Rhenish on my head once'.

clue.text: Beginnings of speeches in codex, or dialectical argument

explanation.surface: Openings of orations found in a manuscript or in logical debate.

clue.text: Dr Robert Knox got the body of his work from them

definitions.text: Dr Robert Knox got the body of his work from them

parts.words: Dr Robert Knox got the body of his work from them
parts.note: Knox was the Edinburgh anatomist supplied with corpses by Burke and Hare

explanation.surface: A scholar's work drew its substance from certain sources.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body of his work' seems to mean his output, but Knox literally bought corpses from body-snatchers for dissection.
explanation.definitionFit: Body-snatchers who dug up corpses to sell to anatomists were given this name in the nineteenth century.
